output.title: What bounced addresses are really telling you
output.body:
A bounced address is usually not the real problem. It is a signal that something in the workflow is leaking: a typo at capture, stale CRM data, a bad import, or a list nobody owns closely enough. For a small business owner, the decision is not “should we use AI?” It is “is this a repeatable email and CRM cleanup problem, or just occasional noise that a person can clear faster than any system?”

That distinction matters. If bounces happen often enough to block replies, waste follow-up, or leave records drifting out of date, you have a bounded workflow worth mapping. If not, the fix may be simpler: better forms, a clearer list owner, or a manual review step. AI should not be pushed into a vague mess and asked to be heroic. That rarely ends well.

The practical next step is to look at one week of bounced messages and trace each one back to its source. Note whether it came from a form, an import, a sales reply, or an old record. Then ask one question: would a human need to decide what to retry, suppress, or investigate? If yes, that is a good candidate for a controlled automation discussion. If no, you probably need cleaner input, not more tooling. Human approval should stay on list changes either way.
